17   Q.    Does the Companies’ use of a forecast test year ending December 31, 2026

18         impact the Commission’s review of forecast costs and assumptions underlying

19           their requested revenue increases?

20   A.    Yes. Unlike a historic test year based on actual revenues and costs, a forecast test

21          year is not tethered to actual results. It is based on the Companies’ forecasts of




                    7 Direct Testimony of Andrea Fackler at 36.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 10

 1           future revenues and operating expenses, plant in service and other rate base costs,

 2            capitalization, capital structure, cost of debt, and cost of equity based on thousands

 3           of assumptions, including programs and approaches that may or not reflect the

 4           actual costs the Companies actually will incur in the forecast months of the base

 5           period and in the 2026 test year.

 6                  In  fact,  utilities, in conjunction with a forecast  test year, have every

 7           incentive  to  understate  their revenues and  overstate  their  costs  (expenses,

 8           capitalized costs (CWIP and plant), and deferrals, among others), and costs of

 9            capital to maximize their requested base revenue increases. The practical reality is

10            that these forecast revenues and costs are never trued-up to the actual revenues and

11            costs.  If the actual revenues are greater than the forecast revenues, then the

12         Companies retain the incremental revenues. Similarly, if the Companies actually

13           incur lower capital expenditures and operating expenses than forecast in the test

14           year, then the Companies retain the savings.

15               Given  this context and the opportunities available to manipulate the

16          assumptions and forecast revenues and costs, the Commission should carefully and

17             critically review the assumptions and forecasts driving the requested revenue

18           increases. This is particularly critical when the utilities seek approval for new

19          programs, or include expansions of existing programs, along with significant

20           increases in costs, such as increases in generation, transmission and distribution

21            capital expenditures, generation routine and major outage maintenance expenses,

22           transmission  and  distribution  maintenance  expenses,  and when  they  seek

23            significant increases in payroll and benefits expenses, including the underlying                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 11

 1            staffing levels by comparing those costs to the history and trendline of actual costs

 2           incurred in prior periods and increases in other costs, such as depreciation expense.

 3                        II. RATE BASE AND CAPITALIZATION ISSUES

 4   A.    Rate Base, Not Capitalization, Is The Most Accurate Approach To Calculate
 5        The Return On Component Of The Base Revenue Requirement

 6   Q.    Describe the Companies’ request to use capitalization in lieu of rate base to

 7           calculate the return on component of the base revenue requirement.

 8   A.    The Companies used capitalization to calculate the return on component of the base

 9          revenue requirements and the requested increases in these proceedings. The

10         Companies also calculated rate base, but used the rate base calculations solely to

11            allocate KU’s total capitalization between the retail and wholesale jurisdictions and

12        LG&E’s total capitalization between electric and gas operations.

13               The Companies’ calculations of capitalization and rate base result in

14           differences  in  the return on component of  the revenue requirement. More

15            specifically, KU calculated jurisdictional capitalization of $6,186.150 million and

16            rate base of $6,096.080 million, a difference of $90.071 million.8 LG&E electric

17           calculated capitalization of $3,738.941 million and rate base of $3,744,344 million,

18          a difference of negative $5.403 million.9 LG&E gas calculated capitalization of

19          $1,414.828 million and rate base of $1,368.785 million, a difference of $46.043

20            million.10



                    8 Capitalization is shown on Schedule A and rate base is shown on Schedule B-1 in each Company’s
         filing.
                    9 Capitalization is shown on Schedule A and rate base is shown on Schedule B-1 on the electric
       schedules in LG&E’s filing.
                    10 Capitalization is shown on Schedule A and rate base is shown on Schedule B-1 on the gas                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 12

 1   Q.    Has the Commission previously addressed and approved the use of rate base

 2          as superior to capitalization to calculate the return on component of the base

 3         revenue requirement for other utilities?

 4   A.    Yes. The Commission now consistently uses rate base to calculate the return on

 5         component of the base revenue requirement for all large investor-owned utilities

 6           subject to its ratemaking jurisdiction, with the exception of KU and LG&E. Most

 7            recently, the Commission approved the change to rate base from capitalization for

 8        KPC, despite its opposition.11 In its Order, the Commission stated:

 9               Based upon a review of the case record and being otherwise sufficiently
10                  advised, the Commission finds that applying the capitalization method to
11                   calculate Kentucky Power’s revenue requirement is not reasonable because
12                     this method measures the capital allocations to Kentucky Power from its
13                  parent company, in excess of that needed to finance Kentucky Power’s
14                    direct investment rate base as determined herein. In the converse, the rate
15                 base method measures the direct investment into Kentucky Power’s system,
16                  and, under the facts presented here, is a more accurate method of measuring
17                  the financial health of Kentucky Power and its operations. For these reasons,
18                  the Commission finds that rate base methodology should be used to
19                 determine revenue requirement for this proceeding. (footnote omitted).12

20                   Prior to adopting this change for KPC, the Commission approved the

21          change from capitalization to rate base at DEK’s request for its gas and electric

22           operations in Case Nos. 2018-00261 and 2019-00271, respectively. In addition to

23        now using rate base for KPC and DEK gas and electric, the Commission historically

24          has used rate base instead of capitalization for Atmos, Columbia, Delta, and KAW.





       schedules in LG&E’s filing.

                    12 Id.                                                                   Lane Kollen

 1   Q.   What reasons did Duke Energy Kentucky provide in support of its request to

 2         change to rate base from capitalization for its gas and electric operations?

 3   A.     In the DEK gas rate case, DEK witness Sara E. Lawler, Director Rates &

 4          Regulatory Planning of Duke Energy Business Services LLC, stated in Direct

 5         Testimony the “Company believes that using gas rate base to calculate the revenue

 6          requirement is the simplest and most transparent method.”13

 7                  In the DEK electric rate case, two other DEK witnesses testified the use of

 8            rate base was superior to the use of capitalization. More specifically, Amy Spiller,

 9           the CEO of DEK, stated in Direct Testimony the following:

10                    Historically, the Company's electric base rates have been determined with
11                  reference to a return on capitalization. Although this methodology may have
12                been appropriate in the past, another methodology is more common today.
13                   Specifically, and as evident in other Duke Energy Kentucky jurisdictions, a
14                   return-on-rate base approach provides a transparent and effective way to
15                   establish base rates. The Commission recently approved the return-on-rate
16                 base approach for the Company's natural gas base rates in Case No. 2018-
17                 00261.14

18                  In addition, William Don Wathen, Jr., Director of Rates and Regulatory

19           Strategy for Ohio and Kentucky, stated in Direct Testimony the “use of rate base is

20          a more precise method for measuring the Company’s actual investment in facilities

21         and equipment to provide utility service” and that “the rate base methodology is an

22            easier and more conventional way to represent investment in utility plant that is not

23           only accepted by this Commission, but throughout the country.”15

 1   Q.   Why is the use of rate base superior to capitalization to calculate the return on

 2         component of the base revenue requirement?

 3   A.    The use of rate base is more precise and accurate than capitalization to calculate the

 4           return on component of the base revenue requirement. It allows the Commission to

 5            specifically review, assess, and quantify each of the costs that will earn a return on,

 6           including those costs that are subtracted from rate base, such as net liability

 7          accumulated deferred income taxes (ADIT) and negative cash working capital

 8        (CWC), the normal result when CWC is properly calculated using the lead/lag

 9          approach and correctly excludes non-cash expenses.

10              The use of rate base also avoids the need to reconcile capitalization to rate

11          base as a reasonableness test when using capitalization for the return on component

12           of the revenue requirement. The rate base approach inherently assumes that

13            capitalization is equivalent to the adjusted rate base authorized by the Commission

14            rather than starting with per books capitalization and making adjustments that may

15           or may not reflect the adjustments made directly by the Commission to the per

16         books rate base.16 The inherent assumption that capitalization equals the adjusted

17            rate base also is reflected in rider filings that use the rate base approach, such as the

18         Companies’ ECR filings and RAR filings. Yet, in the Companies’ base rate case

19             filings, the rate base and capitalization never are equal, regardless of whether there

20         was or is a historic test year or a forecast test year, and regardless of the Companies’




                    16 Capitalization is used only to calculate the capital structure and the weighted cost of capital, which,
        in turn, is applied to rate base. This approach inherently equivalences capitalization to rate base as the basis
        for the return on component of the revenue requirement.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 15

 1           attempts to adjust capitalization to more closely parallel its proposed adjustments

 2            to per books rate base.

 3                  In a  forecast  test  year,  the  per books and  adjusted  rate base and

 4            capitalization amounts never are the same for one or more of the following reasons:

 5           1) equity and debt financings are seldom issued to precisely match the timing of

 6            rate base investment, 2) capitalization reflects financing for amounts that are not

 7          allowed or included in rate base because they are not allowed a rate of return, they

 8           are subject to recovery through a rider that has a true-up mechanism, the costs are

 9            volatile from month to month, or there is vendor financing, among others reasons,

10           3) capitalization does not reflect financing for amounts that the utility seeks to

11           include in rate base, either because the amount included in rate base is a non-cash

12         amount that was not financed or the financing costs are embedded into an expense

13          amount, such as pension and OPEB expense, 4) the forecasts of the rate base

14         amounts and capitalization amounts use different methodologies, 5) short term debt

15           varies daily and generally is much higher on average than the month end short term

16          debt amounts used to calculate the 13- month average capitalization, and 6) other

17           reasons.

18                  In summary, the change to rate base from capitalization for the return on

19         component of the base revenue requirement will ensure consistent treatment for all

20           calculations of the Companies’ revenue requirements, both the base revenue

21          requirements and all of the rider revenue requirements that include a rate base

22          component, including, presently, the ECR and RAR, and, if authorized in this

23           proceeding, the proposed new MC2 and MC6 riders.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 16

 1   Q.    Did the Companies provide a reconciliation between capitalization and rate

 2          base for the test year?

 3   A.    Yes. The Companies provided these reconciliations in their Minimum Filing

 4          Requirements (MFR)17 and provided additional detail for certain line items in

 5          response to AG-KIUC discovery.

 6   Q.   What do these reconciliations demonstrate?

 7   A.    They demonstrate the use of rate base is a more precise and accurate approach. The

 8          use of capitalization is less precise and less accurate because it is essentially a

 9            simplistic “all-in” approach calculated as total assets less total liabilities other than

10            capitalization, albeit with certain limited ratemaking adjustments. Of course, not all

11            assets and liabilities are cash costs nor should all assets and liabilities be included

12          (added if an asset or subtracted if a liability) in the calculation of the return on

13         component of the revenue requirement. This is readily apparent from even a cursory

14          review of each Companies’ reconciliation of capitalization and rate base where

15           there are many assets and many liabilities from the Company’s balance sheet

16          accounts that are not included in the calculation of rate base, but are included in

17            capitalization under the “all-in” approach, albeit with certain limited ratemaking

18           adjustments.

19   Q.   What is your recommendation?

20   A.      I recommend the Commission calculate the return on component of the base

21          revenue requirement using rate base rather than capitalization for the reasons I

 3                  In addition to using rate base instead of capitalization, I recommend the

 4         Commission make a series of corrections to the Companies’ calculations of rate

 9   Q.   What are the effects of your recommendations to use rate base instead of

18   B.    Rate Base And Capitalization Should Be Reduced To Remove Generation And
19         Transmission CWIP;  The  Construction  Financing  Costs  Should  Be
20          Capitalized As AFUDC

21   Q.    Describe the Companies’ requests for current recovery of construction

22          financing costs.

23   A.    The Companies seek current recovery of construction financing costs before the

24           construction is completed and placed in service instead of capitalizing these costs                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 18

 1           as AFUDC, including the AFUDC in CWIP, and then recovering the costs,

 2           including the AFUDC, over the service lives of the assets after construction is

 3          completed and the CWIP is closed to plant in service. The Companies do not seek

 4           current recovery of the financing costs for certain generation and other CWIP

 5           projects the Commission previously approved for AFUDC.

 6   Q.    Describe the AFUDC approach for capitalizing financing costs incurred

 7         during construction.

 8   A.    The financing costs incurred during construction are capitalized and added to the

 9           cost of CWIP under the AFDUC approach, then included in plant in service when

10           construction is completed. The financing costs are computed at the Company’s

11         embedded weighted cost of capital in accordance with the requirements of the

12          Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) methodology set forth in the

13         Uniform System of Accounts (USOA), unless the methodology is modified for

14             retail ratemaking purposes. The FERC methodology requires that the Company’s

15           short-term debt first be assigned to the financing costs for construction and then

16           requires the use of the weighted average cost of long-term debt, preferred equity,

17         and common equity for the residual amount of financing costs.

18   Q.    Will the Companies fully recover their construction financing costs under the

19      AFUDC approach?

20   A.    Yes. The AFUDC approach provides the Companies dollar for dollar recovery of

21            their actual construction financing costs, no more and no  less. In  fact, the

22         Companies proposed and the Commission authorized the use of AFUDC for the

23         Mercer Solar and Mill Creek 5 resources in CPCN Case 2022--00402.  The                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 19

 1         Companies proposed and the Commission authorized the use of AFUDC for their

 2       AMI buildouts in the prior base rate Cases 2020-00349 and 2020-00350. The

 3         Companies also proposed the use of AFUDC for the Brown 12, Mill Creek 6, and

 4         Cane run BESS resources in CPCN Case 2025-00045.

 5              The Companies recognized the legitimacy and usefulness of the AFUDC

 6          approach for new resources in the three CPCN and base rate proceedings as one

 7          element of their proposed ratemaking for the costs of those resources. Among other

 8           benefits of the AFUDC approach, the construction financing costs are recovered

 9          over the service lives of the assets, rather than prematurely recovered over a

10            relatively short construction period and before the assets are completed or provide

11            service.

12                        It makes sense to broaden the use of the AFUDC approach to all generation

13         and transmission construction costs rather than applying it on an ad hoc basis and

14          only to certain construction projects. The ad hoc approach results in a hybrid form

15           of ratemaking and accounting, using AFUDC for certain construction projects and

16       CWIP in rate base for  all other construction projects. This hybrid form of

17          ratemaking is not necessary or rational either for ratemaking or for accounting

18           purposes. Nor is it consistent with the exclusive use of the AFUDC approach by

19           the Commission for other investor-owned utilities, including DEK and KPC.

20   Q.     Is the AFUDC approach consistent with generally accepted accounting

21          principles?

22   A.    Yes. GAAP generally requires that construction financing costs be capitalized into

23           the cost of an asset because such costs are no different in concept than the cost of                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 20

 1           labor and materials used to construct an asset and because the cost has future

 2         economic  value.  Statement  of  Financial  Accounting  Standards  No.  34,

 3           Capitalization of Interest Cost, states the following:

 4                  39.   The Board concluded that interest cost is a part of the cost of
 5                  acquiring an asset if a period of time is required in which to carry out the
 6                     activities necessary to get it ready for its intended use. In reaching this
 7                  conclusion, the Board considered that the point in time at which an asset is
 8                 ready for its intended use is critical in determining its acquisition cost.
 9                 Assets are expected to provide future economic benefits, and the notion of
10                 expected future economic benefits implies fitness for a particular purpose.
11                Although assets may be capable of being applied to a variety of possible
12                   uses, the use intended by the enterprise in deciding to acquire an asset has
13                an important bearing on the nature and value of the economic benefits that
14                           it will yield.
15
16                  40.   Some assets are ready for their intended use when purchased. Others
17                  are constructed or otherwise developed for a particular use by a series of
18                     activities whereby diverse resources are combined to form a new asset or a
19                    less valuable resource  is transformed into a more valuable resource.
20                   Activities take time for their accomplishment. During the period of time
21                   required, the expenditures for the materials, labor, and other resources used
22                   in creating the asset must be financed. Financing has a cost. The cost may
23                  take the form of explicit interest on borrowed funds, or it may take the form
24                  of a return foregone on an alternative use of funds, but regardless of the
25               form it takes, a financing cost is necessarily incurred. On the premise that
26                  the historical cost of acquiring an asset should include all costs necessarily
27                 incurred to bring it to the condition and location necessary for its intended
28                   use, the Board concluded that, in principle, the cost incurred in financing
29                  expenditures for an asset during a required construction or development
30                 period is itself a part of the asset’s historical acquisition cost. (emphasis
31                  added).

32   Q.   How does the CWIP approach differ from the GAAP requirement to capitalize

33          carrying costs in the plant costs and then depreciate the plant costs over the

34           useful service life of the asset?

35   A.    The CWIP approach provides accelerated recovery to the utility of the construction

36           financing cost subset of total construction costs solely during the construction                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 21

 1           period rather than the AFUDC approach, which provides no recovery during the

 2           construction period, but provides recovery over the service lives of the assets. The

 3       CWIP approach is unique to regulated utilities and is available to utilities only if

 4          they are allowed to prematurely recover construction financing costs through CWIP

 5            in rate base during the construction period. On long lead time construction projects,

 6           the CWIP approach may allow a utility to recover as much as 30% or 40% of the

 7             total construction costs during the construction period.

 8              The AFUDC approach  is  consistent with the GAAP requirement  to

 9            capitalize construction financing costs and then depreciate the costs over the asset’s

10           service life. In that manner, the recovery occurs over the service life. The revenue

11          requirement is set to recover the depreciation expense plus a return on the declining

12            capitalization/rate base as the asset is depreciated for book accounting and tax

13           purposes. On long lead time construction projects, the AFUDC approach allocates

14           the total cost over the service life of the assets to the customers who are served by

15           the asset.

16   Q.     Is there a harm to customers from the continued use of the CWIP approach

17          instead of the AFUDC approach?

18   A.    Yes. The CWIP approach causes immediate and continuing economic harm

19         compared to the AFUDC approach on both a nominal and present value basis

20            starting during the construction period and continuing throughout the entirety of the

21            asset’s service life. The economic harm is caused by an asset ADIT for the tax

22            effect of tax/book temporary differences. More specifically, federal tax law requires

23           the utility to capitalize interest using a debt rate of return on the entirety of the                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 22

 1       CWIP balance during construction. This requirement increases the tax basis of the

 2            asset compared to the book cost of the asset. Under the CWIP approach, none of

 3           the actual interest incurred is capitalized to the book basis because it is expensed as

 4           incurred. Under the AFUDC approach the interest incurred is capitalized to CWIP

 5          (book basis) as AFUDC – borrowed funds, thus resulting in a lower asset ADIT

 6          included in rate base and lower cost to customers, all else equal.

 7               Under the CWIP approach, the asset ADIT is greater than under the AFUDC

 8          approach and harms customers through increased costs not only during the

 9           construction period, but also over the entire service life of the asset. The AFUDC

10          approach avoids this incremental and unnecessary cost.

11   Q.    Does the CWIP in rate base approach further harm customers if they have a

12          higher cost of capital than the utility?

13   A.    Yes. The CWIP in rate base approach requires customers essentially to finance on

14           behalf of the utility at their higher marginal cost of capital in lieu of the utility’s

15          lower weighted average cost of capital. The cost of consumer credit card debt is

16          approximately 30% compared to KU’s requested 7.92% WACC and LG&E’s

17           requested 7.80% WACC. Many businesses have a minimum internal rate of return

18           of 30% or more to invest in new capital projects. The CWIP approach essentially

19          imposes a higher cost on customers than the AFUDC approach simply because the

20             utility is able to finance at extremely low costs due to its status as a monopoly

21           subject to rate regulation.

22   Q.   What is your recommendation?                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 23

 1   A.      I recommend the Commission exclude all generation and transmission CWIP from

 2            rate base (if the AG and KIUC recommendation to use rate base is adopted) or

 3            capitalization (if the AG and KIUC recommendation to use rate base is not adopted)

 4         and direct the Companies to accrue AFUDC on the generation and transmission

 5       CWIP projects not already excluded from CWIP in rate base starting with the date

 6        when base rates are reset in this proceeding.

 7              The AFUDC approach is beneficial to the Companies and their customers.

 8               It benefits the Companies because it allows them to capitalize and recover the

 9            entirety of their generation and transmission construction financing costs, no more

10         and no less. It benefits customers because it avoids the premature recovery of these

11           costs during the construction period before the assets provide service, minimizes

12          base rate increases, and allows customers to pay for the construction financing costs

13          over the service lives of the assets when they are used and useful.

14              The AFUDC approach is also lower cost than the CWIP in rate base

15          approach on both a nominal and present value basis due to the return on the higher

16            asset ADIT under the CWIP in rate base approach. The AFUDC approach also

17          provides customers the benefits of the utility’s lower cost of financing not only

18          throughout the construction period, but also continuing throughout the service lives

19           of the assets.

20   Q.   What are the effects of your recommendation?

21   A.    The effects are a reduction in the KU revenue requirement of $25.038 million, a

22           reduction in the LG&E electric revenue requirement of $11.258 million, and a

23           reduction in the LG&E gas revenue requirement of $3.361 million.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 24

 1   C.    Rate Base Is Overstated: Corrections Are Necessary

 2                             1. Summary of Corrections to Rate Base

 3   Q.   What corrections to the Companies’ calculations of rate base are necessary?

 4   A.    The Companies’ calculations of rate base are overstated due to at least five errors,

 5         which I first summarize and then explain in more detail. First, cash working capital

 6        (CWC) should be  corrected  to exclude  all non-cash  expenses,  and, more

 7            specifically, corrected to exclude all depreciation expense, amortization expense,

 8           deferred income tax expense, and non-cash fuel-coal expense. This is consistent

 9          with the Commission Orders and/or utility filings in other investor owned utility

10          base rate proceedings wherein CWC was calculated using the lead/lag approach

11         and all non-cash expenses were excluded.

12                Second, all pension and OPEB related assets and liabilities should be

13          excluded from rate base. The Companies did not finance these balance sheet

14          amounts, except to the extent the returns on the trust fund assets and the interest

15          expense on the obligations are already specifically reflected in the calculations of

16          pension and OPEB costs in accordance with GAAP and USOA accounting

17           requirements. There are no additional financing costs to recover. The Commission

18          should exclude all pension and OPEB related assets and liabilities from rate base

19           consistent with its decision to do so in Case No. 2020-00174. I also note that a

20           portion of the pension and OPEB costs is included in expense and another portion

21             is capitalized to CWIP and plant in service. If the Commission does not exclude all

22          pension and OPEB related assets and liabilities from rate base, then it should at

23            least exclude the amounts related to and allocable to CWIP and plant in service.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 25

 1                  Third, account 184 Pension Clearing Account should be excluded from the

 2            rate base calculation for the simple reason  that under the clearing account

 3          conceptual structure, all costs accumulated in account 184 are charged out to other

 4            capital and expense accounts so that the balance averages to $0 over time.  If the

 5           clearing account is operating correctly, then in some months there may be a small

 6            asset or small liability balance, but, again, the balance by design and practice should

 7          averages to $0 over time and be set to $0 for ratemaking purposes.

 8                    2. Overview of Companies’ Cash Working Capital Calculations

 9   Q.    Provide an overview of the Companies’ calculation of CWC.

10   A.    The Companies’ calculation of CWC consists primarily of two components

11            identified as “Cash Working Capital (Lead/Lag)” and “Cash Working Capital

12          (Balance Sheet Items).” The balance sheet items typically are not identified by

13             utilities as “cash working capital,” but rather typically are identified as “working

14            capital” in order to distinguish the CWC based on the leads and lags in revenues

15         and expenses from the balance sheet items included in rate base. Nevertheless, I

16            will use the Companies’ terminology to address the problems with their calculations

17         and the corrections that are necessary.

18              The Companies’ CWC  (lead/lag) component  is based on a  lead/lag

19          approach that calculates the net investor supplied funds (positive) or customer

20           supplied funds (negative) based on the average daily revenues and expenses using

21           lead days and lag days. The Companies included both cash expenses and non-cash

22          expenses in the calculation of this component, despite the Commission precedent

23            to  exclude   all  non-cash  expenses.  Companies  witness  Andrea  Fackler                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 26

 1         acknowledged the Commission precedent, but included the non-cash expenses

 2          anyway.18

 3          KU included $38.306 million in rate base for this first CWC (lead/lag)

 4          component, of which $54.788 million is for non-cash depreciation, amortization,

 5         and deferred income tax expenses, and LG&E included $19.223 million (electric),

 6           of which $35.563 million is for depreciation, amortization, and deferred income tax

 7          expenses, and $1.730 million (gas), of which $8.653 million is for depreciation,

 8           amortization, and deferred income tax expenses.19 Simply removing the non-cash

 9           depreciation, amortization, and deferred income tax expenses from the Companies’

10           calculations of CWC (lead/lag) turns their positive amounts (additions to rate base)

11            into negative amounts (subtractions from rate base).

12                For ease of reference in my explanations of the Companies’ errors and my

13         recommendations to correct those errors, I have replicated the following tables from

14           the Companies’ calculations of the CWC (lead/lag) components separately for KU,

15       LG&E electric, and LG&E gas.20

 3                       I subsequently address each of the errors included in the Companies’

 4           calculations of the two CWC components. The preceding tables provide ease of

 5           reference to the Companies’ schedules as I sequentially address the errors.

 6               2. Depreciation, Amortization, And Deferred Income Tax Expenses Are
 7           Inherently Non-Cash Expenses That Should Be Excluded From The CWC
 8                           (Lead/Lag) Component Of Rate Base

 9   Q.    Should the Commission include depreciation, amortization, and deferred

10         income tax expenses in the CWC (lead/lag) component?                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 33

 1   A.    No. These are non-cash expenses. The Commission has repeatedly found that non-

 2          cash expenses should be excluded from the CWC calculations. The non-cash

 3          expenses include, but are not limited to, depreciation, amortization, and deferred

 4         income expenses.

 5   Q.    Does the Companies’ use of 0 expense lag days correctly reflect the non-cash

 6          character of these expenses?

 7   A.    No. The Companies should exclude all non-cash expenses. The Companies’ use of

 8         0 expense lag days in lieu of properly excluding these expenses still results in CWC

 9         amounts included in rate base instead of $0 for these expenses. The Companies’

10          use of 0 days is incorrect because it assumes that the depreciation, amortization,

11         and deferred income tax expenses actually are paid in cash and paid in cash

12           instantaneously at the beginning of the month in which the expenses are recorded.

13         These assumptions are unequivocally wrong because the Companies never disburse

14          cash for these expenses, let alone instantaneously.

15              The Companies disburse cash only one time - when they acquire and pay

16            for the underlying assets, whether plant in service, prepayments, regulatory assets,

17          miscellaneous  deferred  debits,  and/or  other  assets.  The  depreciation  and

18           amortization expenses are simply the non-cash allocation of the asset costs recorded

19            to expense for accounting purposes over the service lives of the assets or the

20           amortization periods for other costs.

21                   Similarly, the Companies disburse cash only one time for income tax

22          expense. This cash disbursement is recorded in current income tax expense. There

23           are no cash disbursements for deferred income tax expense.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 34

 1   Q.   What is the correct expense lag days if non-cash expenses are included in the

 2      CWC (lead/lag) calculations?

 3   A.      If non-cash expenses are included in the CWC (lead/lag) calculations, which I

 4           strongly oppose and the Commission has previously denied, then the correct

 5          expense lag days is infinity days, which properly assumes the non-cash expenses

 6           are never paid in cash. If the non-cash expenses are included rather than properly

 7          excluded, but with infinity expense lag days, then the expense lag days far exceed

 8           the revenue lag days and the amount included in rate base will never be greater than

 9           $0, the same result as if the non-cash expenses were properly excluded altogether.

10   Q.   What  is  your  recommendation  regarding  the  non-cash  depreciation,

11          amortization, and deferred income tax expenses?

12   A.      I recommend the Commission exclude these expenses from the Companies’

13           calculations of CWC (lead/lag). These are inherently non-cash expenses. The

14            related balance sheet amounts that required cash disbursements are separately

15          included in rate base and properly earn a return on in that manner. The Commission

16          has already decided these issues in numerous other utility proceedings and should

17             treat the issues in these proceedings consistently with the Orders in the other utility

18           proceedings.

19   Q.   What are the effects of your recommendations?

20   A.    The effects are a reduction in the KU revenue requirement of $5.512 million, a

21           reduction in the LG&E electric revenue requirements of $3.589 million, and a

22           reduction in the LG&E gas revenue requirements of $0.873 million.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 35

 1              3. Fuel-Coal Expense Is Inherently A Non-Cash Expense That Should Be
 2                            Excluded From CWC (Lead/Lag)

 3   Q.    Should the Commission also exclude the non-cash fuel-coal expenses from the

 4      CWC (lead/lag) component?

 5   A.    Yes. The fuel-coal expense also is inherently a non-cash expense. There is no cash

 6         working capital requirement for the fuel-coal expense incurred by KU and LG&E

 7             electric. The fuel-coal expense represents an allocation of the balance sheet fuel-

 8           coal inventory amounts recorded to expense for accounting purposes as the fuel-

 9           coal inventory is consumed. The only disbursement of cash occurs when the fuel-

10           coal inventories are purchased and the vendor is subsequently paid. The balance

11           sheet fuel inventories are already included as separate components in the rate base.

12          There is no second disbursement of cash when the inventories are consumed and

13          recorded to expense.

14   Q.   Do the Companies’ calculations and the expense lag days for the fuel-coal

15         expense correctly reflect the fact this expense is a non-cash expense?

16   A.    No. The fuel-coal expense is a non-cash expense and is not properly included in the

17      CWC (lead/lag) regardless of the claimed expense lag days. KU assumed 36.77

18          expense lag days and LG&E electric assumed 36.67 expense lag days for the fuel-

19           coal expense. However, there are and can be no expense lag days for non-cash

20          expenses. The payment lag for the balance sheet fuel inventories is measured by

21           the related accounts payable and related disbursement of cash for the purchases of

22           coal and oil fuel inventories, which is properly subtracted from the coal fuel

23           inventories included in rate base.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 36

 1   Q.   What is your recommendation regarding the non-cash fuel-coal expense?

 2   A.      I recommend the Commission exclude this expense from the calculation of CWC

 3            (lead/lag). This is a non-cash expense. The inventory costs and related accounts

 4          payable are already separately included in rate base.

 5   Q.   What are the effects of your recommendations?

 6   A.    The effects are a reduction in the KU revenue requirement of $0.851 million and a

 7           reduction in the LG&E electric revenue requirements of $0.581 million.

 6   Q.    Describe the amounts included in account 128 Prepaid Pension.

 7   A.    These amounts included in account 128 represent the net excess of the pension trust

 8          fund assets at fair value over the pension benefit obligation.22 The asset amounts

 9          included in account 128 means the pension trust funds are overfunded compared to

10           the present value of the pension liabilities.

11   Q.   How do  the pension (and OPEB)  trust funds become overfunded or

12         underfunded?

13   A.    The net pension funding amounts in account 128 and the OPEB underfunding in

14          account 228.3 are the net of the pension trust fund assets offset by the pension

15           obligation (present value of the future pension liability), and the net of the OPEB

16             trust fund assets offset the OPEB obligation (present value of the future OPEB

17             liability).

18              The pension trust fund and pension obligations and OPEB trust fund and

19       OPEB obligations were forecast for the test year based on the Companies’ actuarial

20           return assumptions calculated specifically for these rate case proceedings, outside




                    22 Response to AG-KIUC 1-85(b).  I have attached a copy of all parts of the response from KU
        (narrative and selected pages only) as Exhibit LK-3. I have not attached a copy of the response from LG&E
        in the interest of limiting the pages in the exhibit.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 38

 1           of the normal course of business, and were not developed by their actuary for actual

 2          accounting purposes. The pension trust fund is funded and becomes overfunded

 3          through 1) the cumulative actual and forecast realized gains in trust fund assets, 2)

 4          cumulative  actual and  forecast earnings on  trust fund investments, and  3)

 5          cumulative  actual  and  forecast  contributions  and  payments made by  the

 6         Companies.

 7              The pension and OPEB obligation components also affect the calculations

 8           of the net funded status. The pension obligation is increased each year based on the

 9         Companies’ actuarial discount rate assumptions and forecast changes in employee

10            related pay and other actuarial obligations and reduced by actual and forecast future

11         payments to participants discounted to the present value liability using the actuarial

12           discount rate. The OPEB obligation is increased each year based on the Companies’

13            actuarial  discount  rate  assumptions and  forecast  changes  in  the  actuarial

14           obligations, reduced by actual and forecast future payments to or on behalf of

15            participants discounted to the present value liability using the actuarial discount

16             rate.

17   Q.     Is it reasonable to include the pension trust fund assets in excess of the pension

18          obligation in rate base or subtract the OPEB obligation in excess of the OPEB

19           trust fund assets from rate base?

20   A.    No. First, and perhaps most importantly, the Companies have provided no evidence

21            that the excess trust fund assets were solely, or in any respect, the result of excessive

22           contributions by  the Companies.  In  response  to AG-KIUC  discovery,  the

23         Companies acknowledged that the excess trust fund assets include realized and                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 39

 1           unrealized gains in the trust fund assets, earnings on the trust fund assets, and

 2          changes in the pension obligation.23 In fact, these other factors have reduced the

 3        minimum contributions required by the Companies under the ERISA minimum

 4          funding requirements to the point where the Companies will make no contributions

 5            to the pension fund this year or in the test year.24 Second, to the extent the excess

 6             trust fund assets were the result of realized and unrealized gains and realized

 7           earnings, then the Companies’ customers are entitled to the reductions in pension

 8           costs resulting from those sources; the Companies are not somehow entitled to

 9           include those accumulated gains and earnings in rate base. Third, the trust fund

10            assets earn a return within the GAAP formula used to calculate pension costs.25

11           Fourth, the Company did not finance the pension amounts in account 128, nor did

12          customers finance the OPEB amounts in account 228.3. In their most recent rate

13           cases, neither KPC nor DEK added or subtracted these amounts from rate base.

14   Q.    Describe the amounts in account 184 Pension Clearing Accounts.

17   Q.   What are clearing accounts?

18   A.     Clearing accounts are used to accumulate costs for certain activities, such as vehicle

19            costs, which then are charged out to expense or capital based on various allocation

20           or usage factors, such as square footage for building costs or daily usage for vehicle

21            costs. The objective with clearing accounts is to charge out each month an amount




                    31 Responses to AG-KIUC 2-11 in Cases 2020-00349 and 2020-00350.  I have attached a copy of
       the narrative portion of the responses as Exhibit LK-7.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 45

 1           equivalent to the costs incurred and recorded in the clearing account so that the

 2          balance is $0 on average over time, recognizing that in any single month the

 3         amounts incurred and the amounts charged out may not precisely match.

 4              The FERC Uniform System of Accounts (“USOA”) defines account 184

 5          Clearing Accounts as follows.

 6                 This [account] shall include undistributed balances in clearing accounts at
 7                  the date of the balance sheet. Balances in clearing account shall be
 8                   substantially cleared not later than the end of the calendar year unless items
 9                 held therein relate to a future period.

10   Q.   What is the basis for the Companies’ forecast of the account 184 amounts in

11          the test year?

12   A.    The Companies simply used the actual amounts as of February 28, 2025 and held

13           the amounts constant through the end of the test year.32

14   Q.     Is that a reasonable basis for the forecast of the account 184 amounts in the

15            test year?

16   A.    No. There is no conceptual basis for assuming that a clearing account balance will

17          remain the same for 22 months from February 2025 through December 2026. All

18           clearing accounts should be forecast and included at $0 in the test year, consistent

19          with the manner in which such accounts are used and consistent with the

20           expectation that the accounts will be cleared to $0 on average over time.

21   Q.   What is your recommendation?

 1   A.      I recommend that the Commission either set the clearing accounts to $0 or simply

19   Q.    Are the pension expenses for the DB plan reasonable?

20   A.    No. The pension expenses for the DB plan are overstated. The calculations are




                    55 Response to AG-KIUC 1-74.
                    56 Id.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 59

 1          fundamentally flawed and  biased based on  the Companies’  directions and

 2          assumptions provided to the actuary. First, the return on assets credit component of

 3           the pension costs is understated because the trust funds at the beginning of the test

 4          year are understated. If the pension trust funds are understated, the return on those

 5             trust fund assets is understated. The Companies’ use of a February 2025 valuation

 6           date fails to reflect the subsequent significant increases in equity market valuations,

 7           as measured by the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P’s 500, NASDAQ, and

 8           other indices, all of which are at record or near record highs. These valuation

 9           increases will be reflected in the actual pension cost calculations by the Companies’

10           actuary for 2026, which will drive the actual pension expense down in 2026 for

11          accounting purposes compared to the forecast calculated expressly and solely for

12           these rate cases.

13                Second, the return on assets credit component of the pension costs is

14           understated because the Companies reduced the return on the trust fund assets for

15           the  estimate  calculated  expressly and  solely  for  these  rate  cases. Without

16           explanation in witness testimony or in the MFR schedules and workpapers, the

17         Companies directed the actuary to reduce the return on the trust fund assets from

18           the present assumption of 8.25% through the end of 2025 to 7.25% in the test year

19            specifically for these rate cases.57 At the same time, the Companies directed the

20           actuary to retain the present assumption of 5.3% for the discount rate applied to the

21           future pension payments to calculate the present value of the pension obligation




                    57 Id.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 60

 1            specifically for these rate cases.58 It is highly unusual to reduce the return on the

 2             trust fund assets and not reduce the discount rate concurrently due to the direct

 3           correlation between both rates, but that is what the Companies directed the actuary

 4            to do. As a result, the return on trust fund assets credit (negative) component of the

 5          expense calculation was decreased and the calculated pension cost increased, while

 6            at the same time, the interest expense component stayed the same, all else equal.

19   D.    Generating Unit Decommissioning Expense Should Not Be Recovered Until
20          After The Unit Is Retired

21   Q.    Describe the Companies’ request to recover generating unit terminal net

22          salvage (decommissioning expense) in the requested depreciation rates and

23          expense.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 64

 1   A.    The Companies have included estimates of future decommissioning costs in their

 2           requested depreciation rates and expense. Company witness John Spanos describes

 3           the use of an estimated $40/kW current dollar cost for decommissioning coal and

 4           gas-fired generating units and related facilities.65 Witness Spanos then escalated the

 5           current dollar estimated cost to a future dollar estimated cost at the probable

 6           retirement date for each generating unit using a 2.5% annual escalation rate for this

 7           purpose.  Witness Spanos divided the decommissioning cost by the gross plant

 8          remaining after estimated interim retirements and then weighted the terminal and

 9           interim net salvage rates to develop a combined net salvage rate. Witness Spanos

10          then multiplied the combined net salvage rate times the gross plant in each account

11            at the study date and added the resulting net negative salvage to the net plant at the

12          study date to calculate the total cost to be recovered over the average remaining

13           service life of each account for each generating unit.

14   Q.    Did the Commission previously deny recovery of decommissioning expense for

18           gas, and oil fired) generating unit plant accounts, stating: “The Commission also

19           finds that terminal net salvage should be removed from the depreciation rates due

20            to the requirements of KRS 278.264(2) that the Commission ‘shall not . . . take any

21           other action which authorizes or allows for the recovery of costs for the retirement

 1           of an electric generating unit…unless the presumption created by this section is

 9   Q.    Has the Commission considered the decommissioning expense issue for the

10        Companies since KRS 278.264 was enacted?

11   A.    No.

12   Q.    Does KRS 278.264 preclude recovery of decommissioning expense prior to

13          seeking and obtaining Commission approval to retire a specific thermal

14          generating unit?

15   A.    Yes. The statute requires a utility to seek and obtain approval to retire a specific

16          thermal generating unit. There are various thresholds the utility must meet before

17           the Commission may approve a requested retirement. The statute also precludes

18          recovery of decommissioning costs until after the Commission approves the

19           retirement.



                66 Case No. 2022-00372, Electronic Application of Duke Energy Kentucky, Inc. for 1) An

 1            KRS 278.264(1)  states specifically  that, “Prior to  retiring an  electric

 4           application.” The Company has not filed an Application for any of its generating

 5            units, although the Commission approved the retirement of Ghent 2 prior to the

 6          enactment of the statute in Case 2022-00402.

 7            KRS 278.264(2) states: “There shall be a rebuttable presumption against the

 8           retirement of a fossil fuel-fired electric generating unit. The commission shall not

 9          approve the retirement of an electric generating unit, authorize a surcharge for

10           the decommissioning of the unit, or take any other action which authorizes or

11          allows for the recovery of costs for the retirement of an electric generating unit,

12           including any  stranded  asset  recovery, unless the presumption created by this

13           section is rebutted by evidence sufficient for the commission to find that: (a) The

15           generating capacity that: 1.) Is dispatchable by   either the utility or the regional

16           transmission organization or independent system operator responsible for balancing

17          load within the utility’s service area; 2.) Maintains or improves the reliability and

18            resilience of the electric transmission grid; 3.) Maintains the minimum reserve

19           capacity requirement established by the utility’s reliability coordinator; and, 4.) Has

20           the same or higher capacity value and net capability, unless the  utility can

21          demonstrate that such capacity value and net capability is not necessary to provide

22            reliable service; (b) The retirement will not harm the utility’s ratepayers by causing

23           the utility to incur any net incremental costs to be recovered from ratepayers that                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 67

 1          could be avoided by continuing to operate the electric generating unit proposed

 2            for retirement in compliance with applicable law; (c) The decision to  retire the

 9           or decommissioning of the existing unit earlier.”

10            KRS 278.264(3) states that, “The utility shall at a minimum provide the

11         commission with evidence of all known direct and indirect costs of retiring the

12            electric generating unit and demonstrate that cost savings will result to customers

14   Q.    Have any of the Companies’ witnesses addressed the requirements of KRS

15          278.264?

16   A.    No. The Companies intentionally and admittedly decided to ignore and not address

17           the  effects of  this  statute  in  their testimony.67 Witness Christopher Garrett

18           apparently made this decision and communicated it to Witness Spanos via email,68

19           but did not address the effects of the statute in his testimony. Witness Spanos agreed

20          with the Companies, but did not address the effects of the statute in his testimony.69



                    67 Refer to responses to AG-KIUC 1-101(b). I have attached a copy only of the KU response and
       attachment as Exhibit LK-23 due to the volume of the attachment and the fact the attachments are the same.
                    68 Id.
                    69 Id.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 68

 1          Despite these decisions by Witness Garrett and Witness Spanos, the Companies

 2         had Witness Spanos quantify the effects of excluding the terminal net salvage for

 3           the thermal generating units and for all generating units so they had an estimate of

 4           the magnitude of the issue.70

 5   Q.    Even without the statutory prohibition against recovery of terminal net

 6          salvage for the thermal generating units that have not been approved for

 7          retirement, are there reasons why decommissioning expense should not be

 8          recovered prior to the retirement of any of the generating units, regardless of

 9         whether they are thermal or non-thermal generating units?

10   A.    Yes. First, the decommissioning cost is inherently not known or measurable. The

11           costs are estimates of costs many years into the future.

12                Second, recovery of decommissioning costs prior to cash disbursements for

13          such costs after the generating units actually are retired results in a temporary

14           difference for book and tax purposes because the decommissioning expense for

15         book purposes is not deductible for income tax purposes. This temporary difference

16            results in a decommissioning accumulated deferred tax asset (DTA), which is

17          included by the Company in rate base and capitalization because  it has to be

18           financed. This is a cost that is unnecessary and can be completely avoided simply

19         by delaying recovery of decommissioning costs until they actually are incurred and

20           deductible for income tax purposes after the generating unit is retired.

21                  Third,  delayed  recovery  of  decommissioning  expense  promotes




                    70 Id.                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 69

 1           intergenerational equity among customers now and in the future. Generating units

 2           are retired when they are no longer economic and are replaced with lower cost

 3           generation, that generally  is more efficient and has lower fuel and non-fuel

 4           operating expenses. The cost of decommissioning is thus a transition cost to the

 5          newer, more efficient, and lower cost replacement generation and appropriately

 6          recovered from the customers who benefit from the new replacement generation.

 7   Q.   What is your recommendation?

 8   A.      I recommend the Commission deny recovery of all decommissioning expense, not

 9          only for the Companies’ thermal generating units, but also for the solar generating,

10          hydro, and wind facilities.

 1   Q.   What do you recommend?

 2   A.      I recommend the Commission modify the forecast life spans for the coal-fired

 3           generating units so they are consistent and rationalized for depreciation rate and

 4          expense purposes. These generating units are extremely and increasingly valuable

 5            in the PJM capacity markets and in comparison to the costs of new replacement

 6           generation. The Companies will continue to operate these generating units until

 7          they are uneconomic compared to the costs of new replacement generation. The

 8         Commission should recognize this reality in the forecast life spans.

 9              More specifically, I recommend the Commission modify the life spans for

10           the Ghent units so that all four of the units reflect the same life span of 60 years,

11           the forecast life span for Ghent 1 reflected in the requested depreciation rates. This

12            will extend the depreciable life by 3 years for Ghent 2, 4 years for Ghent 3, and 7

13           years for Ghent 4.

15           Solar and Simpsonville Solar Array 1, Simpsonville Solar Array 2, Simpsonville

16           Solar Array 3, and Simpsonville Solar Array 4 from 25 years to 30 years, the same

17           as the forecast life span for future solar assets recommend by Witness Spanos. This

18            will extend the depreciable life by 5 years for the Brown and Simpsonville Solar

19          Arrays so that all solar resources are depreciated using the same 30-year life span.

20                  In addition, I recommend the Commission modify the life span for all of the

21           existing gas-fired combined cycle and combustion turbine generating units, except

22            for the Haefling units, from 40 years to 45 years, the same as the forecast life span

23            that I recommend for the future combined cycle generating units, namely, Mill                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 75

 1         Creek 5, which is presently under construction, and Brown 12 and Mill Creek 6,

 2         which have pending requests for CPCNs in Case 2025-00045. The Company’s

 3          proposed 40 years life span for all gas-fired generating units is unnecessarily and

 4          unduly short and results in excessive depreciation rates and expense. The life spans

 5            for the existing gas-fired generating units should be reviewed and assessed together

 6          with the Companies’ proposed life spans for the future generating units to ensure

 7            that they are consistent and that the effects of adding the future generating units are

10         and the Companies will continue to operate them until they are no longer economic

11            in comparison to new replacement generating units. I address the reasons for the

12          45-year life spans for the future combined cycle generating units in a subsequent

13           section of my testimony.

 4   F.      If Allowed, Decommissioning Expense Should Be Recovered As A Separate
 5         Standalone Expense, Reflect The AG-KIUC Life Span Recommendations,
 6       And Escalated Only Through The End Of The Test Year

 7   Q.     If the Commission allows recovery of decommissioning expense for any of the

 8          generating units, should it be included as a component of the depreciation

 9          rates?

10   A.    No.    It should be included as a separate standalone expense. Including the

11          decommissioning  in  the  depreciation  rates  and  expense  overstates  the

12          decommissioning cost compared to a properly calculated standalone expense.

13                 This occurs because the decommissioning cost is included in the calculation

14           of depreciation rates based on the gross plant at the depreciation study date, in this

15           case, June 30, 2024. Those depreciation rates then are applied to the much greater

16           gross plant in the test year compared to the plant at the study, which necessarily

17            results  in a proportionately greater and excessive decommissioning expense

18         compared to the amount included in the depreciation study and depreciation rates.

19                 This problem is eliminated  if the expense is included as a standalone

20          expense instead of in the calculation of the depreciation rates and then the

21           depreciation expense in the test year.

22   Q.     If the Commission allows recovery of decommissioning expense for any of the

23          generating units, should it reflect the remaining average service life based on

24          the life spans you recommend?                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 77

 1   A.    Yes. If the Commission allows recovery of decommissioning expense, then  it

 2          should reflect the same life spans and other parameters as the depreciation rates and

 3          expense, excluding terminal net negative salvage.

 4   Q.     If the Commission allows recovery of decommissioning expense for any of the

 5          generating units, should it reflect escalation of the decommissioning cost to

 6          future dollars beyond the end of the test year?

 7   A.    No. The Companies escalated the estimated decommissioning costs from current

 8            dollars at the date of the depreciation study to the probable retirement dates for each

 9           of the generating units, many years beyond the end of the test year. This creates a

10            significant mismatch between the revenues and other costs included in the test year,

11         which are limited to the test year and don’t include growth in revenues due to

12          customer growth beyond the end of the test year or growth in any other expenses

13         beyond the end of the test year. The longer the escalation period, the greater the

14          decommissioning cost and the greater the mismatch with all other revenues and

15           costs in the test year. Also, in contrast to the forecast of gross plant in the test year,

16         which is based on the Company’s budget process and reasonably known and

17            certain, the retirement dates for the Company’s generating units are not known and

18            certain, nor is the cost in future dollars tied to the retirement dates known and

19            certain.

20              To illustrate this point more specifically, the Companies included forecast

21          decommissioning costs in 2066 dollars for Trimble County 2, some 40 years after

22           the 2026  test  year  in  this  proceeding.  The Companies  included  forecast

23          decommissioning costs in 2055 dollars for Cane Run 7, some 29 years after the                                                                   Lane Kollen
                                                                         Page 78

 1         2026 test year in this proceeding.

 2   Q.     If the Commission allows decommissioning expense for any of the generating

 3           units, what is your recommendation?

 4   A.    To  reiterate,  I  do  not  recommend  the  Commission  allow  recovery  of

 5          decommissioning  expense  for any  of  the  generating  units  until  after  the

 6         Commission has expressly authorized the retirement of each thermal generating

 7            unit or the actual retirement date of any other non-thermal generating unit.

 8               However, if the Commission allows decommissioning expense for any of

 9           the generating units prior to their retirement and prior to actually incurring any costs

10            for this purpose, then I recommend it calculate the expense as a standalone and

11           separate expense to ensure that the expense is not overstated in the test year due to

12           the methodological problem that I described from including the expense in the

13           depreciation rates based on a study date prior to the test year.

14                       I also recommend the Commission reflect the remaining average service

15            lives for each generating unit based on the life span parameters that I recommend

16            for each generating unit in the calculation of the depreciation rates. Both the

17          decommissioning expense and the depreciation expense should reflect the same life

18          span parameters.

19                   Finally, I recommend the Commission limit the escalation of the current

20            dollar decommissioning cost estimates to the end of the test year to ensure that

21           present rates do not reflect forecasts of estimated decommissioning costs in 2055

22         and 2066 dollars.

23   Q.     If the Commission allows recovery of decommissioning expense for any of the                                                                   Lane Kollen

 5           depreciation expense, for KU, there would be $8.968 million (maximum) in

11          decommissioning and increase in rate base, including the effects of ADIT, and a
